title: Preregistered Paired Evaluation of a Deterministic Verifier Pipeline for LLM‑Generated Network Configuration Changes — Non‑informative Result under Shared‑Generation Semantics
abstract: We report a fully preregistered, archived paired experiment (cand-2026-01-prereg-v1) that tested whether deterministic verifier augmentation (generate → deterministic_netops_validator_v5 → optional repair) reduces verifier‑detected unsafe intent→configuration proposals from a hosted LLM on synthetic NetOps tasks. Design: N=200 preregistered intent→configuration tasks in a paired design comparing (a) baseline LLM‑only and (b) guarded pipeline (gpt‑5‑mini + deterministic validator). Execution used shared_initial_candidate semantics (one LLM call per task) producing model_calls_used = 200 (preregistered independent per‑arm generation budgeted up to 400). Observed (adversarial cluster): baseline SAFE = 200/200; guarded SAFE = 200/200 (paired contingency n11 = 200, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0). Paired SAFE‑rate difference = 0.0; exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0; paired bootstrap 95% CI = [0.0,0.0] (resamples = 10,000, seed = 1729). Because identical per‑pair generations were produced and the observed baseline unsafe rate was 0%, the preregistered causal hypothesis (that a deterministic verifier reduces unsafe proposals) was not testable in this execution. We publish the complete preregistered run and artifacts, diagnose the execution/testability failure, and give concrete, artifact‑supported recommendations (independent per‑arm generation budgeting, adversarial calibration, exploratory ROC reserve use) for informative repeats. All execution and analysis artifacts cited here are archived in the supplied bundle and referenced throughout the text.

sections.introduction: Automating the translation from operator intent into device configuration with large language models (LLMs) promises productivity gains for network operations (NetOps). Incorrect, misordered, or policy‑violating changes can cause outages, violate security intent, or break reachability; deterministic validators and execute‑in‑sandbox patterns are therefore proposed to reduce operational risk. Prior literature reports that tool‑augmentation or generate–validate–repair pipelines can improve measured correctness on curated tasks, but trade‑offs (false refusals, missed unsafe proposals) and evaluation design choices remain open. We preregistered a confirmatory paired experiment to quantify whether a deterministic verifier reduces unsafe configuration proposals produced by a hosted LLM under adversarial prompting. Research question: How does deterministic tool‑augmentation (generate → deterministic validator → optional repair) change the rate of verifier‑detected unsafe proposals produced by a hosted LLM under benign and adversarial NetOps prompts? Contributions: (1) a complete, archived preregistered paired run (cand-2026-01-prereg-v1) comparing baseline LLM‑only vs guarded verifier pipeline on N=200 tasks; (2) an artifact‑grounded diagnosis explaining why this execution was non‑informative for the preregistered estimand (shared generation semantics + zero baseline unsafe rate + no repairs applied = ceiling/testability failure); (3) concrete, archive‑supported recommendations for informative repeats (independent per‑arm generation, adversarial calibration, exploratory ROC estimation) together with precise budget accounting derived from the preregistration and execution artifacts.
sections.related_work: Recent surveys and prototypes demonstrate active research on LLMs for NetOps/AIOps (intent translation, configuration synthesis, remediation planning) and on tool‑augmented agentic workflows. Several works propose generate–validate–repair or divide–verify–refine pipelines and report improvements on domain tasks, but typically on curated or prototype benchmarks rather than workflow‑centred, sandboxed evaluations. Guardrail and red‑teaming literature emphasizes governance and the need for replayable, deterministic scoring traces to measure operational trade‑offs. Our study differs by publishing a fully preregistered, deterministic paired run and focusing on how concrete execution semantics (shared vs independent generation), model‑call budgeting, and verifier application rules interact with the paired estimand and testability. Rather than claiming broad verifier efficacy, we contribute a reproducible worked example that makes explicit how budget and semantics can render a confirmatory design untestable and how to fix it.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and estimand. The study cand-2026-01-prereg-v1 declared a paired binary estimand: paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline computed from deterministic validator labels (1 = SAFE, 0 = UNSAFE). Primary confirmatory test: exact two‑sided McNemar test implemented by paired_binary_analysis_v1; inferential CI: paired bootstrap percentile (10,000 resamples, seed 1729). Sampling and power: preregistration targeted N=200 paired tasks to detect ≈7 percentage‑point paired reductions (assumed baseline ≈10–15%, power 80%, alpha 0.05) and reserved up to 50 exploratory tasks for ROC/refusal estimation.

Task generation and scope. A deterministic task generator (deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5) produced 200 synthetic intent→configuration tasks (per‑task generator seeds 1..200). Tasks targeted IPv4 reachability and simple device‑level workflow constraints limited to fields {admin, mtu, vlan} across multi‑device single‑AS topologies; each manifest includes initial_state, expected_final_state, explicit required_sequence, and allowed_touched_fields. Adversarial prompt variants were created via a preregistered obfuscation template to increase difficulty. All task manifests and representative examples are archived under execution/task_manifest.jsonl.

Compared pipelines and generation semantics. Baseline: LLM candidate accepted and scored post hoc by deterministic_netops_validator_v5. Guarded: the same LLM candidate validated by deterministic_netops_validator_v5 in a deterministic sandbox; the preregistration allowed a single automatic repair call in guarded episodes. Crucially, the preregistration permitted two generation semantics: (A) independent per‑arm generation (two independent LLM calls per task) or (B) shared_initial_candidate (one LLM call per task scored by both arms). The executed run used shared_initial_candidate semantics to conserve hosted model budget (see execution accounting below). The verifier applied scoring_rule = full_intent_constraint_validation and produced structured validation_before/after traces used to derive the binary SAFE/UNSAFE labels.

Execution, retries, and accounting. Execution used requested_model = "gpt-5-mini" and the hosted_netops_gvr_v1 adapter harness. The run followed preregistered retry and exclusion rules (one automatic retry per failed call, deterministic exclusion/replacement for contaminated tasks); no technical failures or exclusions occurred. The execution manifest records planned_episode_count = 400 (200 paired episodes × 2 arms), completed_episode_count = 400, model_calls_used = 200, and maximum_model_calls (preregistered budget for independent generation) = 400. The single shared call per paired task produced identical candidates for both arms; no repairs were applied in confirmatory episodes (repair_provider_trace fields are null in the archived scoring JSONs). All execution and configuration artifacts are archived (paths cited below).
sections.results:
Execution accounting and primary contingency. Execution artifacts record model_calls_used = 200 while the preregistered independent per‑arm generation budget would have allowed up to 400 calls (see execution/execution_manifest.json and execution/model_configuration.json). Deterministic reconciliation and provider audit confirm hosted_model_call_event_count = 200 and that deterministic consistency checks passed.

Confirmatory outcomes. The analysis executor paired_binary_analysis_v1 produced the contingency counts and inferential outputs (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv, analysis/condition_summary.csv). Observed counts (adversarial cluster): n11 (SAFE both arms) = 200; n10 = 0; n01 = 0; n00 = 0. Baseline SAFE = 200/200; guarded SAFE = 200/200. Paired SAFE‑rate difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.0. Exact McNemar two‑sided test p = 1.0. Paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI = [0.0, 0.0] (10,000 resamples, seed 1729). These results are verbatim from analysis/results.json and archived CSV artifacts.

Representative artifacts and repair traces. Representative scoring JSONs (e.g., execution/scoring/task-000001-baseline.json and task-000001-guarded.json) show identical shared_initial_candidate contents and validator traces with violation_count = 0 and validator.valid = true in both validation_before and validation_after. Representative shared responses (execution/responses/task-000001-shared-initial.txt, task-000002-shared-initial.txt, task-000003-shared-initial.txt) contain the canonical per‑pair generated configurations. No repair_provider_trace entries appear for confirmatory episodes, confirming that guarded validation did not cause arm‑level output divergence.

Exploratory reserve unused. The preregistered exploratory reserve (up to 50 tasks) intended for verifier ROC/refusal calibration was not consumed prior to the confirmatory run; analysis/contamination_summary.csv shows no contamination flags and missingness_summary.csv reports zero technical failures or exclusions.
sections.discussion:
Artifact‑grounded diagnosis of the non‑informative execution. Three archived facts together explain why the preregistered causal hypothesis was not testable in this execution: (1) shared_initial_candidate semantics were executed (execution/model_configuration.json; execution/execution_manifest.json) producing one LLM call per task shared across arms; (2) every sampled shared candidate was labeled SAFE by the deterministic validator (baseline SAFE = 200/200; analysis/condition_summary.csv); (3) no repairs were applied in confirmatory episodes (repair traces null), so no arm‑only divergence could arise. With identical per‑pair generations and zero baseline unsafe rate, a paired McNemar contrast necessarily degenerates to concordant outcomes (n11 = N) and is thus uninformative (p = 1.0, degenerate CI). This is a ceiling/testability failure caused by the interaction of generation semantics, model behaviour on the sampled tasks, and the absence of repair‑induced divergence—not evidence that the verifier lacks utility.

Recommendations for informative repeats (artifact‑supported). The preregistration and execution artifacts motivate concrete remedies: (A) use independent per‑arm generation semantics when the estimand is a paired causal contrast of generator+verifier vs generator alone; for N=200 this requires ≈200 additional LLM calls (the preregistered maximum_model_calls = 400 vs executed 200), explicitly budgeted in execution accounting; (B) reserve and use preregistered exploratory items (up to 50) to estimate verifier ROC and tune adversarial templates until a nonzero baseline unsafe rate (e.g., the 10–15% assumed in the power plan) is observed on a calibration set; (C) if repairs are part of the guarded policy, allow and record repair application so repair‑induced divergence can be counted as arm‑specific effects; (D) if budget prevents independent draws, prioritize arm‑level stochasticity (independent generation) over expanding model panels for the same call budget because discordant pairs are essential to McNemar inference. All budget and sensitivity parameters above are taken from the preregistration and execution artifacts referenced here.

Operational implications and interpretation guidance. Practitioners should not interpret a concordant all‑SAFE paired outcome under shared generation as definitive evidence that verification is unnecessary. Instead, the archive shows how evaluation semantics and budgeting can mask verifier effect. For operational evaluation of agentic NetOps pipelines, we recommend explicit budget accounting, exploratory ROC calibration, and a paired design that preserves arm stochasticity or permits repairs to induce divergence.
sections.conclusion: We executed a fully archived, preregistered paired experiment comparing gpt‑5‑mini baseline generation and a deterministic verifier pipeline on 200 synthetic NetOps tasks. Using shared_initial_candidate semantics and the sampled adversarial templates, every candidate was labeled SAFE by the deterministic validator in both arms (n11 = 200), producing a degenerate paired analysis (paired difference = 0.0; p = 1.0; 95% CI = [0.0,0.0]). This outcome reflects a reproducible ceiling/testability failure rather than a substantive efficacy claim. The scientific contribution is methodological and reproducibility‑centred: (1) a complete preregistered run with deterministic artifacts that permits exact replay; (2) an artifact‑grounded diagnosis of why this execution was non‑informative for the preregistered estimand; and (3) precise, archive‑supported recommendations (independent per‑arm generation budgeting, adversarial calibration, exploratory ROC estimation) required to make a future confirmatory test informative. All execution and analysis artifacts (execution/*, analysis/*) referenced in this paper are archived in the supplied bundle and permit deterministic replication of the run and the diagnosis.

limitations: Synthetic task scope: tasks were deterministic synthetic topologies produced by deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5 and limited to single‑AS, multi‑device setups and fields {admin, mtu, vlan}; results may not generalize to production, multi‑AS, or vendor‑specific features.

Generation semantics executed: the run used shared_initial_candidate (independent_condition_generation = false), producing identical per‑pair generations and creating a ceiling/testability effect when shared candidates were valid.

Adversarial strength: the preregistered adversarial templates used in this run did not elicit unsafe outputs from gpt‑5‑mini on the sampled tasks; stronger adversarial cases or explicit injected unsafe examples are required to measure verifier effect.
Single‑model scope: only the declared model (gpt‑5‑mini) was evaluated; no multi‑model generality is claimed.

Verifier completeness: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 ran deterministically in synthetic sandboxed states; external validation of validator completeness against all real‑world NetOps failure modes is not provided.

Operational external validity: no production deployment, operator‑in‑the‑loop workload measurement, nor multi‑vendor field trials were performed; operator‑cost trade‑offs remain unquantified at scale.
